extracted.intended_audience: press release writers, PR professionals, journalists, communications officers
extracted.subtask_description: Writing the lead (first sentence/paragraph) of a press release so it answers the Five Ws (+ H), follows the inverted-pyramid, and is concise and newsworthy for journalists and SEO/AI indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five Ws + One H checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: The Six Questions: Who, What, Where, When, Why, How (sometimes added).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a checklist in journalism to ensure the lead contains all essential points of a story. Historically taught since at least 1913; Rudyard Kipling famously articulated the six items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead must answer all 5Ws+H
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead (first paragraph or first sentence) should answer all 5Ws + H.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is essential for inverted pyramid structure, reader skim-reading, SEO/AI indexing, and quick journalist evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concision: answer all 5Ws+H in 30 words or fewer
rubrics_metrics.description: A good press release lead: Answers all 5Ws+H in 30 words or fewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concision helps with skim readers, journalist pickup, and SEO. Keep the lead tight while still covering the essentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-load the most newsworthy 'what'
rubrics_metrics.description: A good press release lead: Front-loads the most newsworthy 'what'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the primary news event in the beginning of the lead so readers and journalists immediately see the angle and value of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the actor ('Who') clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: A good press release lead: Identifies the actor (who).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name the actor clearly and avoid burying the actor in passive constructions. Journalists need to know who is responsible or affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify time ('When') precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: A good press release lead: Specifies time (when - is it new?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific dates/times rather than vague terms like 'recently' so the newsworthiness (timeliness) is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify location ('Where')
rubrics_metrics.description: A good press release lead: Specifies location (where - relevance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a location anchor to establish geographic relevance; avoid leaving out a location that matters to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide causal context ('Why') / significance
rubrics_metrics.description: A good press release lead: Provides causal context (why - significance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the event happened or why it matters to convey significance; missing significance weakens the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include method/ mechanism ('How') when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: A good press release lead: May include method (how - especially for science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a brief note on how something occurred or how it works when the method is central to the news (e.g., scientific findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common failures / anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent lead problems: burying the actor (passive voice); vague timing ('recently'); no location anchor; missing significance; confusing who's responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these anti-patterns as checks — avoid passive voice, replace vague timing with specifics, provide a clear location and significance, and make responsibility/actor unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit lead scoring rubric (1 point per W)
rubrics_metrics.description: Score 1 point for each W answered clearly in lead: Who, What, When, Where, Why, How (where relevant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A press release lead scoring 5/6 or 6/6 is considered well-formed. Use this simple checklist scoring to assess completeness of the lead.
